misconceptions.statement: Tying a tight rope above a bleeding wound is the best way to stop bleeding.
misconceptions.why: Films and old stories show tourniquets as the standard answer to any bleeding.
misconceptions.fix: Pressing firmly on the wound with a clean cloth is the first step. A tight band can damage the limb and is only for trained people in life-threatening bleeding.

probe.question: A boy's arm is bleeding from a cut. What should you do first?
probe.wrong_answer: Tie a tight rope above the cut.

misconceptions.root_belief: stronger, more extreme action works better

misconceptions.statement: If a cloth soaks through with blood, you should remove it and put on a fresh one.
misconceptions.why: Students think the soaked cloth is now useless and must be replaced.
misconceptions.fix: Do not remove the soaked cloth because it disturbs the clot. Add more cloth on top and keep pressing.

probe.question: The cloth on a wound is full of blood. What next?
probe.wrong_answer: Remove it and put a new cloth directly on the wound.

misconceptions.root_belief: used things must be replaced to work

misconceptions.statement: Pouring turmeric, ash or toothpaste on a cut heals it and prevents infection.
misconceptions.why: Home remedies are passed down in families as natural antiseptics.
misconceptions.fix: These can bring in germs and cause infection. Wash the cut with clean running water and cover it with a clean dressing.

probe.question: What should you put on a fresh cut to keep germs away?

misconceptions.root_belief: natural or traditional means safe and effective

misconceptions.statement: A cut must be rubbed or scrubbed hard to get it properly clean.
misconceptions.why: Students link cleaning with scrubbing as with dirty clothes or utensils.
misconceptions.fix: Rinse gently under clean running water and pat dry around it. Hard scrubbing hurts the tissue and can restart bleeding.

probe.question: How should you clean a scraped knee?
probe.wrong_answer: Scrub it hard with a cloth until no dirt is visible.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one situation works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: For a nosebleed you should tilt your head back so the blood does not come out.
misconceptions.why: It seems that lifting the head will stop blood from flowing out.
misconceptions.fix: Sit up, lean slightly forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes. Tilting back lets blood run down the throat.

probe.question: A girl has a nosebleed. How should she hold her head?

misconceptions.root_belief: hiding a problem is the same as solving it

misconceptions.statement: Ice or ice-cold water is the best thing to put on a burn.
misconceptions.why: Students think the colder the cooling, the faster the relief.
misconceptions.fix: Use cool running tap water for 10 to 20 minutes. Ice can further damage burnt skin.

probe.question: What should you put on a hot-water burn on the hand?

misconceptions.statement: Sucking out the venom or using a herbal paste from a local healer is enough to treat a snake bite.
misconceptions.why: Stories and local practices suggest that removing venom from the bite or using herbs neutralises it, so hospital care seems optional.
misconceptions.fix: Only antivenom given in a hospital neutralises snake venom. Sucking or herbal remedies do not work and waste precious time. Go to hospital at once.

probe.question: A farmer is bitten by a snake. A villager offers a herbal paste that he says cures snake bites. What should the family do?
probe.wrong_answer: Apply the herbal paste and wait a day; go to hospital only if the swelling gets worse.

misconceptions.root_belief: Traditional home remedies can replace medical treatment
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO snakebite guidance; Government of India national snakebite management protocol

misconceptions.statement: After a snake bite the person should run or walk quickly to the hospital.
misconceptions.why: Students think speed means moving fast on foot, but they forget that movement pumps venom faster through the body.
misconceptions.fix: Keep the person calm and the bitten limb still, and carry or transport them to hospital by vehicle. Walking and running spread the venom faster.

probe.question: A girl is bitten on the leg by a snake and the hospital is 1 km away. How should she get there?
probe.wrong_answer: She should run to the hospital as fast as she can so she gets there sooner.

misconceptions.root_belief: Faster own movement always means faster help
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO snakebite guidance; Government of India national snakebite management protocol

misconceptions.statement: A person who has fainted should be given water or sprinkled with water on the face and made to drink it right away.
misconceptions.why: Films show people being splashed and given water to revive them, so students believe drinking helps wake them up.
misconceptions.fix: Lay the person down and raise their legs. Give nothing to eat or drink until fully awake, as they could choke.

probe.question: A classmate faints in assembly and starts to open their eyes. What do you do first?
probe.wrong_answer: Pour water into their mouth so they drink and recover quickly.

misconceptions.root_belief: Giving drinks revives anyone who feels weak
misconceptions.source_hint: Indian Red Cross / St John first aid manuals

misconceptions.statement: A person who feels faint should be kept sitting or standing upright, with the head held high.
misconceptions.why: Students think upright is the normal healthy position, and lying down looks like giving up.
misconceptions.fix: Fainting happens when blood flow to the brain drops. Lying flat with legs raised helps blood reach the brain.

probe.question: A girl turns pale and says she feels faint. How should she be positioned?
probe.wrong_answer: Make her stand up straight, or hold her upright, and fan her.

misconceptions.root_belief: Upright posture keeps a person alert
misconceptions.source_hint: Indian Red Cross / St John first aid manuals

misconceptions.statement: CPR is done to make the heart start beating again, and it works like a restart button.
misconceptions.why: TV scenes show the person waking up right after compressions, so students think CPR restarts the heart.
misconceptions.fix: CPR only keeps blood and oxygen moving to the brain and organs until help arrives. A defibrillator and medical care are needed to restart a normal heartbeat.

probe.question: After 5 minutes of CPR the person has not woken up. What does this mean?
probe.wrong_answer: CPR has failed, so you should stop because it did not restart the heart.

misconceptions.root_belief: First aid fully cures the problem itself
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO / Indian Resuscitation Council CPR guidance

misconceptions.statement: In an emergency you must call 100 for police, 102 for ambulance and 101 for fire, and there is no single number.
misconceptions.why: Older separate numbers are widely known, so students think each service needs its own number.
misconceptions.fix: 112 is India's single national emergency number for police, fire and ambulance. Separate numbers like 108 also work in many states.

probe.question: A house is on fire and people are injured. Which number can you dial that reaches all services?
probe.wrong_answer: There is none; you must dial 101 for fire, then 102 for ambulance separately.

misconceptions.root_belief: Each emergency service has only its own number
misconceptions.source_hint: Government of India ERSS 112 official information
